item.title: Prospects and limitations of adaptive variational quantum algorithms for lattice field theories: a case study in 2+1 dimensions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the popular ADAPT‑VQE approach, which has already enabled proof‑of‑principle vacuum preparation in one‑dimensional gauge models, runs into two fundamental roadblocks when pushed to realistic 2+1‑D lattice field theories: real‑valued operator pools become blind to gradient information and the algorithm can mistakenly lock onto excited states. By diagnosing these issues with concrete examples—including free Wilson fermions—and demonstrating that adding charge‑conjugation symmetry to the pool (or mixing pools with tailored initial states) restores reliable ground‑state convergence, the work provides the first practical recipe for scaling variational quantum simulations beyond 1+1 dimensions. These insights are crucial for anyone aiming to use near‑term quantum hardware to tackle higher‑dimensional lattice gauge problems, as they clarify both the limits of current methods and concrete steps to overcome them.

The variational quantum algorithm ADAPT-VQE has previously been used to prepare the vacuum of lattice gauge theories in $1+1D$. In this paper, we study whether it extends to higher dimensions. We identify two general limitations of ADAPT-VQE. First, if the qubit Hamiltonian and the initial state are real, i.e., invariant under qubit-level time-reversal, all real-valued pool operators have vanishing gradients and are never selected. Second, the algorithm can converge to excited eigenstates. We illustrate both limitations, also providing examples from literature, and present a first application of ADAPT-VQE to a lattice field theory in $2+1D$, namely free Wilson fermions, where both obstacles occur. Adding charge conjugation symmetry to the operator pool improves the results, and combining different pools with suitable initial states recovers the ground and first excited states over the full mass range. These findings give practical guidelines for applying ADAPT-VQE to lattice field theories beyond $1+1D$.

item.title: A Koashi--Imoto Criterion for Holevo-Rate Visible Compression
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a long‑standing question in quantum source coding by giving an exact, operational condition—via the Koashi–Imoto decomposition—for when the optimal Holevo rate can be reached without entanglement assistance, simply using shared randomness. The result clarifies that for qubit ensembles the only way to hit the Holevo limit is if the signals are all pure or mutually commuting, a restriction that directly informs the design of hardware‑efficient compression protocols and error‑tolerant quantum networking stacks. By linking visible compression to recent recovery and decoupling techniques, it also bridges foundational information theory with practical coding strategies, though the bound shows that any mixed component forces a non‑negligible rate penalty regardless of block length.

For a finite memoryless quantum source whose encoder knows the sequence of classical labels, we determine when the Holevo rate is achievable with shared classical randomness and no shared entanglement. In the maximal Koashi--Imoto decomposition of the signal ensemble, this occurs exactly when each signal is pure on the quantum part of every sector it occupies. For qubits, this means that the signals are all pure or commute pairwise. If any occupied quantum part is mixed, every code with sufficiently small mean local error has rate bounded away from the Holevo information, uniformly in blocklength. To prove the converse, we apply Fawzi--Renner recovery to a hypothetical sequence of visible codes approaching the Holevo rate at vanishing local error, then invoke a decoupling bound of Baghali Khanian and Winter for blind compression.

item.title: Classical algorithms for sparse random Hamiltonians via free probability
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that for a broad class of sparse random Hamiltonians—a setting long thought to demand quantum simulation—classical algorithms can match quantum runtimes up to sub‑exponential precision, narrowing the gap between classical and quantum performance on average‑case many‑body problems. By leveraging free probability to extract long‑time dynamics from short‑time data, the authors sidestep the usual exponential blow‑up associated with sign problems, entanglement growth, or low‑temperature regimes that cripple tensor‑network methods. The result sharpens our understanding of where genuine quantum advantage may lie and suggests new classical tools for benchmarking quantum hardware, though it remains limited to random, non‑local models rather than structured Hamiltonians encountered in chemistry or materials science.

The search for quantum advantage in average-case problems is a pressing open question in physics and computer science. The widest conjectured example of such an advantage is in simulation of quantum many-body systems, where sign problems and entanglement growth cause the breakdown of many classical methods. Nonetheless, theoretical evidence for or against such an advantage remains scarce. Here, we investigate this in sparse random non-local Hamiltonians. We design a classical algorithm for such Hamiltonians that enables accurate computation of spectral fluctuations, thermal values, and time-ordered and out-of-time-order correlation functions. For any subexponential precision $\varepsilon$, our algorithm runs in time $(1/\varepsilon)^{2+o(1)}$, nearly identical to a quantum simulation. Crucially, this applies even at late evolution times, low temperatures, and near critical points, where existing classical methods require exponential time. Rather than directly simulating a quantum state or operator, our algorithm first computes the model's mean behavior and then a short hierarchy of instance-dependent corrections. These corrections predict long-time behavior based on short-time data using free probability theory.

item.title: Class-resolved sifting for quantum key distribution with photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial variables
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how class‑resolved sifting can unlock the full two‑bit per‑pair capacity of photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial modes, turning what was previously treated as separate “high‑dimensional” channels into a single, efficiently usable key source. By analysing each degree of freedom independently yet simultaneously, the authors expose subtle basis‑dependent side‑channels that arise from the measurement apparatus—a diagnostic that is increasingly important as QKD moves toward multi‑degree‑of‑freedom implementations and higher data rates. The technique dovetails with recent advances in orbital‑angular‑momentum and other high‑dimensional QKD schemes, offering a practical pathway to boost key yields while maintaining rigorous security bounds, though its statistical sensitivity still limits detection of very weak cross‑couplings.

Photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial variables can carry two key bits per pair in entanglement-based quantum key distribution. We develop class-resolved sifting for such sources: every detected pair is assigned to a class according to which degrees of freedom were measured in compatible bases, and error and key rates are estimated separately in each class. Applied to previously reported data from a two-crystal spontaneous parametric down-conversion source read out in intermediate fractional-Fourier planes, the method recovers the key yield of independent sifting and turns the comparison between classes into a quantitative consistency test for cross-dependencies between the two degrees of freedom. The measured dependence lies below the spatial-polarization coupling predicted for the source, at the edge of the present statistical sensitivity. Resolving the data by polarization-analyzer setting, we find an approximately twofold dependence of the spatial error on the polarization setting in one readout arm, attributable to the measurement apparatus rather than to the source and relevant to basis-dependent side channels. We compare the hyperentangled protocol with a single 4-dimensional system measured in two mutually unbiased bases. Fundamentally, both yield the same key per detected pair and obey the same entropic bound, but they differ in their tensor-product structure: hyperentanglement factors the bases into separate two-outcome measurements, which are simpler to implement and allow errors to be attributed to each degree of freedom, whereas a single variable gives access to non-product bases that can increase the noise tolerance. For the present source, whose polarization coherence is limited by partial which-crystal erasure, a single-variable spatial encoding would yield more key only if its four-outcome readout kept the symbol error within a few percent.

item.title: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a practical route to simulate light‑matter lattice models on near‑term quantum hardware by combining qubit and bosonic registers in a Trotterized circuit, something that has only recently become feasible with tools like Bosonic Qiskit and matrix‑product‑state backends. By benchmarking single‑polariton transport, two‑excitation dynamics under hard‑core constraints, and entanglement growth against exact diagonalization, the authors show that hybrid qubit‑boson simulations can capture nontrivial many‑body physics while remaining tractable on classical simulators. The work therefore paves the way for experimentalists to explore more complex, possibly open, photonic quantum systems on emerging platforms that natively support both qubits and bosonic modes.

The Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard (JCH) model describes the interaction of light and matter in coupled optical cavities and provides a framework for studying their quantum dynamics. In this work, we design a Trotterized quantum circuit to investigate the real-time dynamics of the JCH model using Bosonic Qiskit and a Matrix Product State (MPS) backend. We simulate single-polariton transport and benchmark site occupations against exact diagonalization results. We then extend the simulations to the two-excitation sector under a hard-core photon constraint, examining excitation transport and symmetry properties. Finally, we study the dependence of bipartite entanglement entropy on the inter-cavity photon-hopping strength. The results illustrate how hybrid qubit-boson circuits, simulated with matrix product states, can be used to study light-matter lattice dynamics. This work provides a numerical benchmark for extending hybrid simulation approaches to more complex interacting and open light-matter systems.

item.title: Perturbative unitarity bounds from qubit entanglement in scalar scattering and QED
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that the entanglement generated between qubit‑encoded particle spins in simple scalar and QED scattering can be used as a quantitative probe of perturbative unitarity, yielding coupling‑constant limits that are often tighter than traditional partial‑wave bounds. By tracing out momentum and analysing the resulting quantum channel, the authors turn a textbook scattering problem into a concrete testbed for quantum information techniques, suggesting new ways to benchmark and validate quantum simulators that aim to emulate relativistic field theories. The approach also sidesteps the notorious forward‑scattering singularities that plague conventional analyses, offering a cleaner theoretical handle that could inform both high‑energy phenomenology and the design of hardware‑efficient algorithms for scattering simulations.

In the framework of $2\to 2$ relativistic scattering described by the perturbative $S$-matrix, we perform a comprehensive analysis of the properties of quantum channels obtained by tracing out the momentum from the scattered state. We work in two distinct scenarios with qubit degrees of freedom: flavored scalar contact interactions and QED, focusing in particular on initial-state leptons with transverse polarization. We identify the conditions that make the quantum channel unitary, calculate the entanglement of the qubits through the concurrence, and use its maximally allowed value to extract perturbativity upper bounds on the coupling constants. We find that the limits are often more constraining than the corresponding partial-wave expansion bounds, and that they allow us to bypass some of the obstacles associated in the latter with the singular behavior of forward scattering.

item.title: Programmable multipartite entanglement analogues
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a reconfigurable metasurface that can program the number and type of coherently linked degrees of freedom in a classical electromagnetic field, achieving Bell‑like and GHZ‑like states up to five parties—the highest multipartite order yet realized in optics without genuine quantum entanglement. By making multipartiteness itself tunable across polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction and envelope modes, the work provides a versatile testbed for probing the structure of complex quantum correlations using lossless, room‑temperature light. It bridges recent advances in programmable photonic metasurfaces with the need for scalable platforms to benchmark multipartite protocols, offering a low‑cost sandbox for algorithm development while reminding readers that the underlying physics remains classical rather than nonlocal.

Quantum entanglement underpins the quantum information science. Its multipartite forms distribute coherence across several subsystems, but controlling their composition and order is increasingly difficult as more subsystems participate. Classical nonseparable waves provide accessible analogues of these structures, although existing implementations largely fix the participating degrees of freedom through their generating architectures. Here we overcome this constraint by making multipartiteness itself programmable in electromagnetic fields. A spatiotemporal metasurface reconfigures the identity and number of coherently linked state spaces independently across polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction, and orthogonal envelope modes. We realize complete Bell-like and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-like families from bipartite to five-partite order and exchange constituents at fixed order. To our knowledge, the five-partite state has the highest multipartite order experimentally realized in classical electromagnetic fields. These results establish the distribution of coherence across physical state spaces as a programmable property of classical waves and provide a platform for studying selected structures of multipartite quantum states without invoking quantum entanglement or nonlocality.

item.title: Classical sampling of verifiable graph-state quantum advantage experiments
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the current “verifiable quantum‑advantage” proposals can still be outpaced by modest classical hardware, underscoring how delicate the balance between verifiability and hardness truly is. By exploiting the built‑in error‑detection structure, the authors classically sampled the 70‑qubit graph‑state experiment with higher fidelity than IBM’s own processor, revealing that T‑gate placement—forced to hide from the verifier—leaves a tractable tail for classical simulators. The work therefore maps a concrete obstacle for future advantage demonstrations and signals that any next‑generation verifiable benchmark must deliberately scramble or conceal non‑Clifford resources to avoid such classical shortcuts.

Quantum computers are expected to outperform classical ones on some tasks, but a convincing demonstration must be both hard to reproduce classically and verifiable. A recent proposal achieves verifiability by preparing graph states with built-in error detection, so that the quality of the experiment can be certified without simulating it; hardness is added by measuring in a non-Clifford basis or by inserting T gates. We show that the two instances posted to demonstrate this proposal on IBM hardware can be sampled classically on eight graphics processing units, with higher quality than the hardware in comparable or shorter time. For the 70-qubit instance our samples are drawn from the ideal output distribution; for the 64-qubit instance with 314 T gates they come with a certified fidelity of at least 0.908, against 0.349 for the hardware. The reason lies in verification itself: T gates can only be placed where the error detection cannot see them, which pushes them towards the end of the circuit, where they add little classical cost. Our results identify the features that future verifiable advantage experiments must control.

item.title: Quantum optimization beyond qubit count by low-energy subspace sampling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent (QSSD), a heuristic that breaks the traditional one‑qubit‑per‑variable bottleneck by using a fixed‑angle QAOA circuit as a low‑energy sampler, allowing problems with thousands of variables to be tackled on devices with only a few hundred qubits. By demonstrating approximation ratios above 0.95 on a 10 000‑variable Max‑cut instance with just 100 circuit runs, the work shows that quantum optimization can begin to scale beyond current hardware limits and may eventually compete with classical heuristics as gate fidelity improves. While QSSD still trails the best classical solvers in raw performance, its slower but problem‑size‑independent runtime points to a promising niche for near‑term quantum processors on large combinatorial tasks.

On current digital quantum devices, standard one-qubit-per-variable encodings restrict quantum optimization algorithms to problem sizes where classical solvers typically excel. To avoid this constraint, we introduce Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent (QSSD), an iterative heuristic that decouples the number of problem variables from qubit count, while preserving knowledge of the problem's global structure. QSSD drives the energy descent using a fixed-angle Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm as a low-energy sampler. As the angles are precomputed, each iteration requires just a single circuit execution. We test QSSD on IBM Heron and Nighthawk quantum devices with up to 152 qubits on instances of higher-order unconstrained binary optimization and Max-cut problems. On the largest instance with 10000 variables, QSSD reaches an approximation ratio above 0.95 with 100 circuit executions. We provide both exact and heuristic classical baselines, namely greedy, branch-and-bound solver, and simulated annealing. While our approach still does not match the performance of the best classical baseline, it shows promise in a slower runtime scaling with problem size given a fixed budget. This suggests a regime of large problems where subspace sampling on quantum devices could become competitive, as we also demonstrate how improvements in hardware will lead to better algorithm performance. QSSD is thus a practical heuristic for combinatorial optimization problems that helps bring quantum optimization a step closer to utility.

item.title: Quantum Capacity with Incoherent Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that when quantum processors are limited to incoherent (basis‑state) encoding—a realistic constraint for many near‑term hardware platforms—even infinitesimal depolarizing noise can collapse the channel’s capacity to zero, meaning no qubit can be transmitted reliably. By deriving a single‑letter Holevo‑information formula and proving that incoherent decoding can at most halve the achievable rate (a bound that is tight), the work provides the first quantitative benchmark for how much performance is sacrificed under such restrictions. The results sharpen our understanding of practical capacity limits and will help guide error‑mitigation strategies as experimentalists design devices that must balance coherence control with hardware simplicity.

Arbitrarily weak depolarizing noise drives the quantum capacity to zero in every input basis when the encoder is restricted to incoherent operations. Even one qubit cannot then be sent reliably: if the output is replaced by the maximally mixed state with probability $\varepsilon\le1/2$, the entanglement fidelity is at most $1-\varepsilon/2$ at every block length. With unrestricted decoding, a single-letter formula gives the capacity with incoherent encoding as the maximum Holevo information over ensembles of basis states with identical environment outputs. For either incoherent or unrestricted encoding, imposing incoherent decoding reduces the capacity by at most a factor of two; this factor is optimal. We bound the fidelity of incoherent decoders and evaluate the capacities with incoherent encoding for multiqubit Pauli channels.

item.title: When Randomness Hides Quantum Simulation Errors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the apparent severity of Trotter‑simulation errors can collapse dramatically when the input states are sufficiently random, with 2‑design ensembles yielding observable errors exponentially smaller than the worst‑case bounds for generic states. By quantifying the transition from 1‑ to 2‑design behavior through the excess frame potential, the authors provide a concrete metric that links state statistics to error visibility and even tighten the required Trotter step count to O(T^{1+3/(4p)}) for pth‑order formulas. The result gives quantum algorithm designers a practical lever—engineering or sampling from random‑like states—to reduce simulation overheads, though it also highlights that such gains depend on maintaining high‑quality randomness in the input ensemble.

Trotter formulas approximate quantum dynamics by discrete steps, but errors in measured observables can be much smaller than worst-case estimates. We investigate how this suppression depends on the degree of randomness in the input states. item.title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that embedding a simple convex‑projection step into machine‑learning error mitigation can guarantee physically valid density matrices while dramatically sharpening the accuracy of noisy quantum simulations. By demonstrating sub‑percent energy errors and state fidelities above 0.99 for realistic three‑ and four‑qubit nuclear bound‑state calculations on IBM hardware, the work proves that careful choice of training data and regression model can turn ML‑QEM into a practical tool for near‑term chemistry and physics problems. Noise in quantum devices remains a major challenge for reliable quantum simulations, making quantum error mitigation an important tool for improving their accuracy. Machine learning-based quantum error mitigation (ML-QEM) provides a useful approach, but its performance depends on the training datasets and may produce reconstructed quantum states that are not physically valid. In this work, we introduce an ML-QEM framework that uses residual learning with convex projection to ensure that reconstructed density matrices satisfy physically valid density matrices. We study the effect of different training datasets and regression models using Haar-random and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) ansatz states. We compare the proposed approach with conventional ML-QEM, readout error mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation. The method is tested on IBM quantum hardware for three- and four-qubit simulations of the bound $Λ$-deuteron and $Λ$-$α$ hypernuclear systems, respectively. For the three-qubit system, ridge regression trained on VQE-ansatz states gives a ground-state energy of -0.134 MeV, close to the ideal value of -0.135 MeV, with a state fidelity of 0.999. For four-qubit system, kernel ridge regression gives ground-state energies of -3.014 and -3.045 MeV, with corresponding state fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998. These results show that physically constrained reconstruction, along with the choice of training datasets and regression models, can improve ML-QEM performance for the quantum simulations studied in this work.

item.title: Second-order asymptotics for the quantum and private capacities of the erasure channel
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first tight second‑order expansion for both the quantum and private capacities of the erasure channel, showing exactly how the achievable rate deviates from the well‑known linear term by a universal √n Gaussian correction that depends on the target infidelity. By proving matching upper bounds for any fixed error probability, it settles a long‑standing gap between achievability and converse in the finite‑blocklength regime—a crucial step for realistic quantum network design where only modest numbers of channel uses are available. The result also dovetails with recent advances in quantum finite‑size analysis and provides a concrete benchmark for developing near‑optimal error‑correcting codes and secret‑key protocols over lossy links.

An erasure channel either delivers a quantum system intact or tells the receiver that it was lost. How much quantum information, or secret classical information, can a finite block transmit without assistance? We determine the optimal second-order coding rates for input dimension $d\ge2$, erasure probability $0<p<1/2$, and fixed infidelity (one minus fidelity) $0<\varepsilon<1$. For $n$ channel uses, the optimal base-two logarithmic code size is \begin{equation}\tag{A}\label{eq:abstract-rate} n(1-2p)\log_2d +2\sqrt{np(1-p)}\log_2d\,Φ^{-1}(\varepsilon) +O((\ln n)^2), \end{equation} where $Φ$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function and $Φ^{-1}$ is its quantile function. The square-root term is the second-order correction. This formula holds for entanglement transmission, entanglement generation, and private classical communication. Quantum error measures failure to preserve entanglement. Private error compares the actual output with a correctly decoded uniform message independent of an optimized environment state. The achievable Gaussian term and a matching quantum expansion below infidelity one half were established recently. We prove matching upper bounds for every fixed infidelity, including private communication, with the displayed remainder. The proof bounds one code's average performance across all loss patterns of a given size; binomial fluctuations then determine the Gaussian correction. It combines tests of correct and secret communication with tensor-product averaging and a classical polynomial identity. Arbitrary mixed encoders and collective decoders are allowed. Requiring the private error bound for every message preserves the Gaussian term. Fixing the ideal environment state to the actual marginal instead changes the quantile to $Φ^{-1}(1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon})$. Thus the precise privacy criterion affects communication at second order.

Preparing thermal states on noisy quantum hardware requires circuits that remain shallow at low temperatures. Even when accurate classical state representations are available, compiling them into suitable circuits can be costly. We introduce PP-VarQITE, combining Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution to determine circuit parameters entirely classically, with target temperatures encoded in the angles of a fixed circuit architecture. In numerical studies of Ising and frustrated Heisenberg models, we recover low-temperature energies and correlations using up to 100 qubits. Across the frustrated chain and two-dimensional lattice, our circuits are approximately two to ten times shallower than the lowest-depth circuits from sequential tensor-network compilation. These shallow circuits enable us to prepare a 48-site frustrated chain and a $7\times7$ Ising lattice using 96 and 98 qubits on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. We reproduce the development of dimer order and lattice-wide correlations from high to low temperatures, with the lattice circuits requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers. item.title: Quantum Coherence and Basis-Dependent Correlations in Quantum Systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints exactly which bipartite states carry no extra coherence beyond what is already present locally, showing that block‑diagonal product structures erase basis‑dependent correlations for both Tsallis‑entropy and quantum‑Fisher‑information coherence measures. By clarifying the structural conditions under which global coherence adds nothing to local resources, it sharpens our understanding of how coherence can be harvested or conserved in multi‑qubit hardware—a key issue as experimental platforms strive to balance entanglement generation against decoherence overhead. Quantum coherence and quantum correlations are two fundamental features of quantum systems and are closely related in various quantum information tasks. In general, due to the existence of correlations, the amount of coherence in a bipartite state should be no less than that in the reduced states. We focus on what types of states have an equal amount of coherence in the global state and the local states. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between the absence of basis-dependent correlations and the block-diagonal product structure in a special case. We then consider the coherence measure based on quantum Fisher information and show that block?diagonal product states again lead to vanishing basis-dependent correlations, while in the two-qubit case the vanishing condition constrains the state to a broader block-diagonal-like product structure. These results provide a structural characterization of bipartite states with vanishing basis-dependent correlations under different coherence measures.

item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a clever LLM‑guided redesign of the RNS arithmetic pipeline can slash the Toffoli count for Shor’s RSA‑2048 attack to under one billion—a milestone that narrows the gap between theoretical attacks and realistic hardware requirements. By delivering a Pareto frontier of qubit‑Toffoli trade‑offs, it builds on Gidney’s 2025 optimizations and demonstrates that automated code‑generation tools can uncover resource savings that hand‑crafted designs miss. Modular exponentiation dominates the logical cost of factoring 2048-bit RSA integers (RSA-2048) with Shor's algorithm. Recent approaches based on approximate residue number systems (RNS) sharply reduce the required logical qubits, yet still demand billions of Toffoli gates. Optimizing these circuits is difficult because shared ancilla qubits and measurement-based uncomputation tightly couple the arithmetic stages, while rare overflows in compressed registers occur too infrequently for random simulation to detect. Here we use large language model (LLM)-driven search to redesign the RNS pipeline across stages and build a deterministic compiler that produces a Pareto frontier of RSA-2048 circuits. We bound rare overflow probabilities analytically and verify the resulting elementary gate sequences across all constituent RNS primes on representative circuits. Relative to Gidney's 2025 baseline under matched adder accounting, our frontier cuts the minimum qubit-Toffoli product by 70.1% and lowers expected factoring Toffolis by up to 78.6% at matched accumulator precision, bringing RSA-2048 factoring below one billion Toffolis for the first time.

The traveling salesman problem (TSP) forms the foundation for many logistics and optimization tasks. At the same time, this problem is NP-hard and requires significant computational resources. Quantum computing promises to substantially accelerate computations or increase solution accuracy. The TSP can be conveniently mapped onto the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulation, which in turn can be solved using variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) methods, but this mapping requires a quadratic number of qubits. The higher-order binary optimization (HOBO) formulation requires significantly fewer qubits, but it contains higher-order terms. In our work, we thoroughly investigate both formulations and provide a practical recipe for solving the TSP. We give a comprehensive study and compare in detail QUBO and HOBO formulations.

item.title: Linear entanglement suffices for $f$-routing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a lingering open question in quantum communication complexity by proving that any Boolean‑controlled routing task can be achieved with only 2n + 2 EPR pairs, bringing the entanglement requirement down from super‑polynomial to linear for all functions f. By shifting the burden to an exponentially long quantum message from Alice while keeping Bob’s side classical, it highlights a concrete trade‑off between shared entanglement and communication bandwidth that will inform the design of future distributed quantum networks. Although the total resource cost remains higher than earlier schemes when both messages and entanglement are counted, the linear bound sharply limits how much entanglement‑saving lower‑bounds can ever be proved, tightening our theoretical understanding of quantum routing protocols.

In $f$-routing, Alice receives an $n$-bit string $x$ and an unknown qubit, and Bob receives an $n$-bit string $y$. They share a state prepared in advance and exchange one simultaneous message each. The party selected by the Boolean function $f(x,y)$ must then recover the unknown qubit without further communication. To perform $f$-routing successfully, Alice and Bob need to share entanglement that scales with $n$ for some functions $f$, but the lower and upper bounds for the entanglement are not tight. This paper shows that $2n+2$ shared EPR pairs suffice for every function $f$. The best previous bound that holds for all functions is a shared state of $2^{O(\sqrt{n\log n})}$ qubits. The new strategy moves the cost from the shared state to the messages: Alice sends an exponentially long message of $2^{n+1}+1$ qubits, while Bob sends only classical bits. When the messages are counted towards the resources as well, the previous strategy remains the cheapest known. The result also limits lower bounds that count only the shared state: they cannot exceed a linear number of EPR pairs. The result is formalized in Lean.

Starting with tuned pulses, we then track errors using gate-set tomography for ten days without recalibration. BIR-4 holds its rotation angle to 0.3 degrees throughout, including across a 1.3MHz frequency jump. Antidegradable quantum channels have zero capacity for reliable quantum communication. However, they can nevertheless transmit quantum information with nontrivial fidelity. This raises the question: how well can quantum information be preserved through such channels? In this work, we exactly characterize the optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity of quantum erasure channels throughout the antidegradable regime. Specifically, we show that it equals $γ+\frac{1-γ}{d}$ for transmission probabilities $0<γ\le \frac{1}{2}$ and logical dimension $d$. We use fractional extendibility to establish an upper bound on the entanglement fidelity achievable by arbitrary error-correcting protocols. Furthermore, we construct a family of permutation-invariant codes that asymptotically saturates this bound.

item.title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints exactly which quantum resources—coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic—are needed to faithfully approximate a given function, moving beyond the generic claim that quantum models are universal approximators. By deriving tight bounds for one‑ and two‑qubit circuits and showing how Clifford‑only training can recover uniform approximation with only polynomial depth overhead, it connects directly to current efforts to design hardware‑efficient quantum machine‑learning algorithms for noisy intermediate‑scale devices. Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.

Curator's Take: This article shows that a simple greedy best‑first search can systematically locate locally equivalent graph states with far fewer edges than previously achievable, directly cutting the number of costly CZ gates and circuit depth needed for measurement‑based quantum computing and repeater networks. By framing the local‑complementation problem as a state‑space search, the authors outperform heavyweight integer‑linear‑programming and local‑search methods across random, bounded‑degree, and LDPC‑derived graphs—an advance that could ease hardware constraints on connectivity and error‑rate budgets. The work also highlights that escaping early local minima is essential, suggesting future algorithmic refinements may further tighten resource overheads for large‑scale quantum architectures.

In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.

item.title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces THeatA, a full‑stack simulation framework that explicitly tracks ion‑by‑ion motional heating during transport and schedules cooling operations, allowing realistic error models for QCCD trapped‑ion processors. By linking the mean phonon number to gate‑dependent error rates, it reveals how shuttling‑induced heating can dominate logical error scaling of surface‑code cycles—information that was missing from prior QEC simulators. The work arrives as several groups are prototyping modular ion traps, giving them a practical tool to balance transport speed, cooling overhead, and fault‑tolerance thresholds. Its current focus on single‑species linear arrays means further extensions will be needed for mixed‑species or two‑dimensional architectures.

The quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture is a promising approach to scalable trapped-ion quantum computing, enabling flexible qubit interactions by transporting ions between dedicated trap zones. Programs for such systems require operations beyond conventional circuit primitives: ion shuttling, physical SWAPs, trap splitting and merging, and cooling. Motional excitation accumulated during transport increases the mean phonon number of ions and degrades the fidelity of the two-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates. However, existing quantum error correction (QEC) simulation frameworks do not jointly track per-ion motional excitation and explicitly schedule cooling operations with their transport time and heating costs. We develop a full-stack software framework for QEC experiments and simulations on linear QCCD systems with a single ion species, comprising an intermediate representation (IR) supporting QCCD-native operations, a compiler that translates syndrome-extraction circuits into the IR, and a heating-aware noise-injection pipeline that generates noisy Stim circuits. The compiler updates the mean phonon number of each ion throughout the schedule, and the pipeline derives gate-dependent error rates from the tracked phonon states and per-ion timing, enabling the evaluation of finite-size logical-error scaling of the rotated surface code under transport- and heating-aware noise. We show that transport-induced heating prevents logical error rates from decreasing with increasing code distance under the evaluated conditions, and that indirectly cooling the ion pairs involved in two-qubit gates, by merging them with precooled coolant ions immediately before each gate, restores this decrease. By sweeping the duration and post-cooling mean phonon number of an abstract cooling instruction, we characterize their trade-off and identify the region in which logical-error scaling is maintained.

item.title: Quantifying superposition via coherence by stochastic orthogonalization
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article provides the first operational bridge between the abstract notion of quantum superposition and the well‑studied resource theory of coherence, showing that stochastic orthogonalization measurements can convert any superposition into a quantifiable amount of coherence. By defining a “degree of superposition” that inherits the operational meaning of existing coherence measures, it offers a practical tool for benchmarking how much useful interference a hardware platform or sensor can actually generate. The work also clarifies fundamental limits—such as why deterministic conversion to maximally coherent states is only possible for up to three reference states—informing both theoretical resource‑theory research and the design of devices that rely on precise superposition control.

Here we present an approach to quantifying superposition of nonorthogonal reference states through quantum coherence. No change of basis achieves this: every orthonormal basis makes some superposition-free states appear coherent. We show that orthogonalization succeeds instead as a measurement mapping every reference state onto a multiple of a basis vector in each outcome; such measurements are exactly the free operations that convert superposition into coherence. The largest average coherence they extract from a state, which we call its degree of superposition, turns every coherence measure into a superposition measure with the same operational meaning. An interference term becomes coherence at most with the probability of unambiguously discriminating its two reference states, a bound attained when there are no others and, for positive coefficients and nonnegative overlaps, exactly when the overlaps are probabilities of a random grouping. Maximal degree means conversion into a maximally coherent state with certainty, possible for up to three reference states but not in general. Each coherence measure gives its own degree; when two degrees order two superpositions oppositely, neither converts into the other with certainty, and we find such pairs already for two reference states, unlike in qubit coherence. For equal positive overlaps, in-phase superpositions are rigid: deterministic conversions that keep all components can only permute their coefficients. As the reference states merge, the degree stays bounded where widely used measures can diverge, and at every amplitude a rotation-symmetric cat state attains its maximum. Our results quantify superposition operationally and reveal conversion constraints created by nonorthogonality.

item.title: Quantum Cyclic XYZ Stabilizer Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a new family of cyclic XYZ stabilizer codes that extend the familiar CSS construction by incorporating Y‑type checks, and it shows how assigning disjoint irreducible factors of \(x^n\!-\!1\) yields explicit codes with provably optimal distances for a given length and dimension. By proving that these codes achieve minimum distances beyond the best known CSS bounds—and even surpass linear‑programming limits—the work demonstrates that non‑CSS, highly symmetric stabilizers can deliver stronger error protection without sacrificing the regular structure prized by hardware designers. The result dovetails with recent pushes toward more versatile fault‑tolerant architectures, suggesting a practical pathway to higher‑performance quantum memories and logical gates built on cyclic, easily implementable circuits.

XYZ codes generalize the Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) framework by adding $\sym{Y}$-type stabilizers to the usual $\sym{X}$- and $\sym{Z}$-type ones. We study XYZ codes whose three classical component codes are binary cyclic codes of odd length~$n$. Assigning disjoint sets of irreducible factors of $x^n-1$ to the three Pauli types fixes the number of encoded logical qubits and ensures that the row spaces of the three parity-check matrices intersect pairwise trivially. Then, a coprimality condition between the factors assigned to each type and the reciprocals of those assigned to the others guarantees the required orthogonality. Cyclotomic cosets give a complete and explicit description of the resulting family. We show that, for odd~$n$, a cyclic stabilizer code admits an XYZ representation with cyclic component codes iff its stabilizer generators are invariant, up to a phase, under the qubit permutation $i\mapsto 2i\bmod n$. By fixing the length and the dimension of the code, the proposed cyclic XYZ codes attain the best known minimum distance of stabilizer codes, exceed the minimum distance of the underlying CSS codes, and even exceed the linear-programming upper bounds for general CSS codes.

item.title: Binary-Tree Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for the Maximum $k$-Cut Problem
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a binary‑tree variant of QAOA that tackles the Max‑k‑Cut problem with only 2k – 3 MaxCut subproblems, dramatically cutting qubit and gate counts compared with conventional k‑level encodings. By showing that the approximation ratio degrades only modestly across successive splits, the authors provide a theoretical guarantee that the method scales gracefully on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices—a key hurdle for applying QAOA to real‑world combinatorial tasks. The work therefore broadens the practical reach of variational algorithms, offering near‑term hardware users a more resource‑efficient pathway to solve multi‑partition graph problems without sacrificing solution quality.

The maximum $k$-cut (Max-$k$-Cut) problem, as a natural generalization of the maximum-cut (MaxCut) problem, has broader applications in practical engineering. To solve this problem on quantum devices, existing studies typically encode the $k$ possible subset assignments of each vertex within the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), which directly causes the required quantum resources to grow substantially with $k$. Here we propose a binary-tree quantum approximate optimization algorithm (BT-QAOA), which solves the Max-$k$-Cut problem by applying standard MaxCut QAOA to at most $2k-3$ subproblems. Specifically, after solving MaxCut once on the full vertex set, each subsequent step splits only the subset that yields the largest cut-value gain. This process is equivalent to constructing a binary tree whose leaf nodes after $k-1$ steps form an approximate solution to the Max-$k$-Cut problem. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the approximation ratio in terms of the single-step splitting quality, showing that the overall approximation ratio does not decay exponentially across multiple splits. Numerical simulations show that BT-QAOA substantially reduces the single-circuit qubit and gate overhead while maintaining a high approximation ratio, improving the estimated success probability of a single compiled circuit by orders of magnitude. This work effectively expands the practical reach of QAOA on near-term quantum hardware, offering a new route for solving more complex real-world optimization problems with limited quantum resources.
